draft.title: Mise en scene
card: Mise en scene (say it "meez on sen") means everything placed in the frame of a shot. It is French for "put on stage". Filmmakers choose each item to build meaning.
Setting is where the shot takes place. Costume is what characters wear. Props are the objects in the scene. Each one tells viewers something about a character or a mood.
Lighting shapes mood. Soft, warm light can feel safe, while harsh light or deep shadow can feel tense or threatening.
Where actors stand also carries meaning. A character placed alone at the edge of the frame, far from a group, can seem excluded.
draft.remember: Mise en scene is everything placed in the frame, and each choice helps build meaning.

a.q: Which choice is part of a shot's mise en scene?
opts: A lamp left on a bare table in a dim room
The order in which two shots are joined
A narrator reading a story over the images
The length of time before a cut to a new shot
a.why: A lamp, a table and a dim room are all placed in the frame, so they are mise en scene. Joining shots in order and cutting after a set time are choices about how shots are put together, not about what is inside one frame.
a.clue: Ask what is inside the frame of a single shot.

b.q: In a school drama, Tara sits alone at one end of a long canteen table. The other students crowd the far end, laughing. What does this placement most likely suggest?
opts: Tara is excluded from the group
Tara is the leader of the group
Tara is happy to be on her own
Tara has just arrived at the school
b.why: Where actors stand carries meaning. Tara placed far from a close, laughing group suggests she is left out. Calling her the leader is tempting because she is set apart, but leaders are usually placed with or in front of a group, not away from it.
b.clue: Think about the distance between Tara and the crowd.

a.best: A lamp left on a bare table in a dim room

b.best: Tara is excluded from the group
